'''''Vitis vinifera''''', the '''common grape vine''', is a species of [[flowering plant]], native to the [[Mediterranean Basin|Mediterranean region]], [[Central Europe]], and southwestern [[Asia]], from [[Morocco]] and [[Portugal]] north to southern [[Germany]] and east to northern [[Iran]].<ref name=emp>{{cite web |website=Euro+Med Plantbase Project |url=http://ww2.bgbm.org/_EuroPlusMed/PTaxonDetail.asp?NameId=34500&PTRefFk=500000 |title=Vitis vinifera |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928003507/http://ww2.bgbm.org/_EuroPlusMed/PTaxonDetail.asp?NameId=34500&PTRefFk=500000 |archive-date=28 September 2007}}</ref> {{as of|2012}}, there were between [[List of grape varieties|5,000 and 10,000 varieties]] of ''Vitis vinifera'' grapes though only a few are of commercial significance for wine and table grape production.<ref name="WSET">{{cite book |publisher=Wine & Spirits Education Trust |title=Wine and Spirits: Understanding Wine Quality |pages=2–5 |edition=Second Revised |date=2012 |location=London |isbn=978-1-905819-15-7}}</ref>

The wild grape is sometimes classified as ''Vitis vinifera'' var. ''sylvestris'' (in some classifications considered ''Vitis sylvestris''), with ''Vitis vinifera'' var ''vinifera'' restricted to cultivated forms. Domesticated vines have [[hermaphrodite#Plants|hermaphrodite]] flowers, but ''V. vinifera'' var. ''sylvestris'' is [[dioecious]] ([[male]] and [[female]] flowers on separate plants) and pollination is required for fruit to develop.

Grapes can be eaten fresh or dried to produce [[raisins]], [[Sultana (grape)#Raisins|sultanas]], and [[Zante currant|currants]]. [[Grape leaves]] are used in the cuisine of many cultures. The fresh grapes can also be processed into [[grape juice|juice]] that is fermented to make [[wine]] and [[vinegar]]. Cultivars of ''Vitis vinifera'' form the basis of the majority of wines produced around the world.  All of the familiar wine varieties belong to ''Vitis vinifera'', which is cultivated on every continent except for [[Antarctica]], and in all the major wine regions of the world.

== History ==
===Prehistory===
Changes in pip (seed) shape (narrower in domesticated forms) and distribution suggest that domestication occurred about 4100–3000 BC,<ref>{{cite news |last=Hotz |first=Robert Lee |date=11 January 2011 |title=Perhaps a Red, 4,100 B.C. |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052748704458204576074141252276326 |access-date=21 August 2016 |newspaper=Wall Street Journal}}</ref> in southwest Asia, [[South Caucasus]] ([[Armenia]]<ref>{{cite magazine |title=6,000-year-old winery found in Armenian cave (Wired UK) |magazine=Wired UK |url=https://www.wired.co.uk/news/archive/2011-01/12/ancient-winery |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208180627/http://www.wired.co.uk/news/archive/2011-01/12/ancient-winery |archive-date=2015-12-08 |access-date=2015-11-01}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite web |author=James Owen |date=2011-01-12 |title=Earliest Known Winery Found in Armenian Cave |url=http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2011/01/110111-oldest-wine-press-making-winery-armenia-science-ucla/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110112152642/http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2011/01/110111-oldest-wine-press-making-winery-armenia-science-ucla/ |archive-date=January 12, 2011 |access-date=2019-04-02 |publisher=National Geographic News}}</ref> and [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]]), or the Western Black Sea shore region ([[Bulgaria]], [[Romania]]). The earliest evidence of domesticated grapes has been found at Gadachrili Gora, near the village of Imiri, [[Marneuli Municipality]], in southeastern [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]]; carbon-dating points to the date of about 6000 BC. The oldest winery in the world (dating to 4100 BC) was found in the [[Areni-1 cave]], which lies in [[Areni]], [[Armenia]].<ref>{{cite web |date=March 1, 2012 |title=Areni-1 Cave, Armenia: A Chalcolithic–Early Bronze Age settlement and ritual site in the southern Caucasus |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/259334407 |access-date=April 10, 2017 |publisher=Research Gate}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> Grape pips dating back to the 5th–4th millennium BC were also found in Shulaveri; others dating back to the 4th millennium BC were also found in Khizanaant Gora. Wild grapes were [[harvest (wine)|harvested]] by neolithic foragers and early farmers. For thousands of years, the [[fruit]] has been harvested for both medicinal and nutritional value; its history is intimately entwined with the [[history of wine]].<ref>{{cite book |title=From Vines to Wines in Classical Rome: A Handbook of Viticulture and Oenology in Rome and the Roman West |author=Thurmond, David L. |publisher= BRILL, 2016 |isbn=978-90-04-33459-5|date= 2016-12-08}}</ref>

===Antiquity===
Cultivation of the domesticated grape spread to other parts of the [[Old World]] in pre-historic or early historic times.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite journal |last1=Batiuk |first1=Stephen D. |year=2013 |title=The fruits of migration: Understanding the 'longue dureé' and the socio-economic relations of the Early Transcaucasian Culture |journal=Journal of Anthropological Archaeology |volume=32 |issue=4 |pages=449–477 |doi=10.1016/j.jaa.2013.08.002}}</ref> The first written accounts of grapes and wine can be found in the ''[[Epic of Gilgamesh]]'', an ancient [[Sumer]]ian text from the 3rd millennium BC. Numerous hieroglyphic references from ancient Egypt also exist, according to which wine was reserved exclusively for priests, state functionaries and the pharaoh.<ref>{{cite book |title=Wine and Society |author=Charters, Steve |publisher=Routledge |year=2006 |isbn=978-1-136-34886-0}}</ref>

The grapevine is referenced 55 times in the [[Hebrew Bible]] (Old Testament), along with grapes and wine, which are also frequently mentioned (55 and 19, respectively).<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last1=Netzer |first1=Yishai |last2=Netzer |first2=Nissan |date=2021 |title=Hebrew Vine and Wine Terms from Ancient Times to the Present |url=https://www.ariel.ac.il/wp/judea-and-samaria-research-studies/2021/07/05/%d7%92%d6%b6%d6%bc%d7%a4%d6%b6%d7%9f-%d7%91%d7%9e%d7%95%d7%91%d7%9f-%d7%92%d6%b8%d6%bc%d7%a4%d6%b6%d7%9f-%d7%9e%d7%95%d7%a0%d7%97%d7%99-%d7%92%d7%a4%d7%9f-%d7%95%d7%99%d7%99%d7%9f-%d7%9e%d7%99%d7%9e/ |journal=Judea and Samaria Research Studies |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=127–145 |doi=10.26351/JSRS/30-1/5 |issn=2617-8737 |s2cid=241465067|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The Bible lists the grapevine as one of the [[Seven Species]] of the [[Land of Israel]],<ref>{{Bibleverse||Deuteronomy|8:8|HE}}</ref><ref name=":12" /> and frequently uses it as a symbol of the [[Israelites]] as the chosen people.<ref>{{Bibleverse|Isaiah|5:7}}, {{Bibleverse|Hosea|9:10}}</ref> A detailed description of vineyard maintenance is provided in the [[Book of Isaiah]] ([[Isaiah 5|5]]:1–7).<ref>{{Citation |last=Walsh |first=Carey Ellen |chapter=The Cultivation of Grape Vines |date=2000-01-01 |title=The Fruit of the Vine |pages=87–126 |chapter-url=https://brill.com/display/book/edcoll/9789004369825/B9789004369825-s005.xml |access-date=2024-07-22 |publisher=Brill |language=en |doi=10.1163/9789004369825_005 |isbn=978-90-04-36982-5|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

[[File:Cup vintage Cdm Paris 320 n4.jpg|thumb|left|Grape harvest on [[Etruscan art|Etruscan]] terracotta from the 6th century BC]]
[[Hesiod]] in his ''[[Works and Days]]'' gives detailed descriptions of grape harvests and wine making techniques, and [[Homer]] also makes many references. Greek colonists then introduced these practices in their colonies, especially in southern Italy ([[Magna Graecia]]), which was even known as Enotria due to its propitious climate.

The [[Etruscans]] improved wine making techniques and developed an export trade even beyond the Mediterranean basin.<ref>{{cite book |title=Etruscan Civilization: A Cultural History |author=Haynes, Sybille |publisher=Getty Publications |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-89236-600-2}}</ref> The ancient Romans further developed the techniques learnt from the Etruscans, as shown by numerous works of literature containing information that remains valid: ''[[De Agri Cultura]]'' (around 160 BC) by [[Cato the Elder]],  ''[[De re rustica (Varro)|De re rustica]]'' by [[Marcus Terentius Varro]], the ''[[Georgics]]'' by [[Virgil]] and ''De re rustica'' by [[Lucius Columella|Columella]].{{citation needed|date=February 2012}}

During the 3rd and 4th centuries AD, the long crisis of the Roman Empire generated instability in the countryside which led to a reduction of viticulture in general, which was mainly sustained only close to towns and cities and along coastlines.{{citation needed|date=February 2012}}

===Medieval era===
Between the 5th and 10th centuries, viticulture was sustained almost exclusively by the different religious orders in monasteries. The Benedictines and others extended the grape growing limit northwards and also planted new vineyards at higher altitudes than was customary before. Apart from 'ecclesiastical' viticulture, there also developed, especially in France, a 'noble' viticulture, practiced by the aristocracy as a symbol of prestige.<ref>{{cite book |title=The Archaeology of Medieval England and Wales |volume=47 |author=Steane, John |publisher=Routledge |year=2014 |isbn=978-1-317-59994-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title= The New Oxford Book of Food Plants |author1= Vaughan, John |author2=Geissler, Catherine  |edition=2nd |publisher= OUP Oxford |year= 2009 |isbn= 978-0-19-160949-7}}</ref> Grape growing was a significant economic activity in the Middle east up to the 7th century, when the [[expansion of Islam]] caused it to decline.<ref>{{cite book |title=Genetics, Genomics, and Breeding of Grapes |editor1=Francoise, Anne |editor2=Blondon, Adam |editor3=Martinez-Zapater, Jose Miguel |editor4=Kole, Chittaranjan |edition=illustrated |publisher=CRC Press |year=2016 |isbn=978-1-4398-7199-7}}</ref>

[[File:Vergy-vignes.jpg|thumb|left|Vineyard in [[Burgundy (French region)|Burgundy]]]]

===Early modern period===
Between the Low Middle Ages and the Renaissance, viticulture began to flourish again. Demographic pressure, population concentration in towns and cities, and the increased spending power of artisans and merchants gave rise to increased investment in viticulture, which became economically feasible once more.{{citation needed|date=February 2012}} Much was written during the Renaissance on grape growing and wine production, favouring a more scientific approach.  This literature can be considered the origin of modern [[ampelography]].{{citation needed|date=February 2012}}

Grapes followed European colonies around the world, coming to [[North America]] around the 17th century, and to [[Africa]], [[South America]] and [[Australia]]. In North America it formed [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]] with native species from the genus ''Vitis''; some of these were intentional hybrids created to combat ''[[phylloxera]]'', an [[insect]] pest which affected the European grapevine to a much greater extent than North American ones and in fact managed to devastate European wine production in a matter of years. Later, North American rootstocks became widely used to graft ''V. vinifera'' cultivars so as to withstand the presence of phylloxera.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://winesociety.stanford.edu/roots-and-time-travel |title=On roots, and time travel | Stanford Wine Society |access-date=18 July 2017 |archive-date=11 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201011172214/https://winesociety.stanford.edu/roots-and-time-travel }}</ref>

In the second half of the 20th century there was a shift in attitude in viticulture from traditional techniques to the scientific method based on fields such as microbiology, chemistry and [[ampelography]]. This change came about also due to changes in economic and cultural aspects and in the way of life and in the consumption habits of wide sectors of the population starting to demand quality products.{{citation needed|date=February 2012}}

==Description==
[[File:Vigne_en_fleur.JPG|thumb|220px|Leaves and inflorescences]]
It is a [[liana]] growing {{convert|12-15|m|ft|round=5|abbr=on}} tall at a fast rate.<ref>[https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/134401/i-Vitis-vinifera-i/Details Vitis vinifera grape vine] by RHS.</ref><ref>[https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=vitis+vinifera vitis vinifera – L.] Plants For A Future.</ref> Having a flaky [[Bark (botany)|bark]], its [[leaf|leaves]] are alternate, palmately lobed, [[deciduous]], with three to five pointed lobes, coarsely prickly-toothed leaf margins and a heart-shaped foot, {{convert|5|-|20|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long and broad. They are glossy dark green on top, light green below, usually hairless.

The vine attaches to supports by [[tendrils]]. The stems, called twigs, grow from their tip, the [[cauline]] apex. A branch consists of several [[Internode (botany)|internode]]s separated by knots, which grow the leaves, flowers, tendrils and between-core and where to train future buds. During their hardening, the twigs become woody branches that can reach a great length.  Its roots usually sink to a depth of two to five meters and sometimes up to 12–15 meters or even more.

The species typically occurs in humid forests and streamsides.

===Inflorescences===
Their flowers, small and greenish to white, are grouped in [[inflorescence]]s and their fruits, of different shapes depending on the subspecies, are berries grouped in clusters. The [[Calyx (botany)|calyx]] is single-leaf with five short, deciduous teeth. The [[corolla (botany)|corolla]] consists of five petals, fused at the top and base, and then falls off in its entirety. Opposite the petals there are five [[stamen]]s interspersed with glands. The upper [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] bears a very short style with a button-shaped [[Stigma (botany)|stigma]]. The wild vine is a [[dioecious]] plant, the male and female flowers arise on different plants, but the cultivated forms are hermaphroditic, allowing [[self-pollination]].

The [[fruit]] is a [[Berry (botany)|berry]], known as a [[grape]] that is ovoid or globular, dark blue or greenish, usually two-locular with five seeds; in the wild species it is {{convert|6|mm|in|frac=32|abbr=on}} diameter and ripens dark purple to blackish with a pale wax bloom; in cultivated plants it is usually much larger, up to {{convert|3|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} long, and can be green, red, or purple (black).

==Distribution==
''V. vinifera'' accounts for the majority of world wine production; all of the most familiar grape varieties used for wine production belong to ''V. vinifera''.<ref>Robinson, Jancis. ''Concise Wine Companion''.  2001, Oxford University Press.</ref>

In [[Europe]], ''Vitis vinifera'' is concentrated in the central and southern regions; in [[Asia]], in the western regions such as [[Anatolia]], the [[Caucasus]], the [[Middle East]], and in [[China]]; in [[Africa]], along the northern [[Mediterranean]] coast and in [[South Africa]]; in [[North America]], in [[California]] and also other areas like [[Michigan]], [[New Mexico]], [[New York (state)|New York]], [[Oregon]], [[Virginia]], [[Washington (state)|Washington state]], [[British Columbia]], [[Baja California ]], [[Ontario]] and [[Québec]]; in [[South America]] in [[Chile]], [[Argentina]], [[Uruguay]], [[Peru]] and [[Brazil]]; and in [[Oceania]] in [[Australia]] and [[New Zealand]].

== Cultivation ==
[[File:Grapess.jpg|thumb|A cultivated Common Grape Vine, ''Vitis vinifera'' subsp. ''vinifera'']]
Use of [[grape]]s is known to date back to [[Neolithic]] times, following the discovery in 1996 of 7,000-year-old [[wine]] storage jars in present-day northern [[Iran]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Berkowitz |first=Mark, The Archaeological Institute of America |url=https://archive.archaeology.org/9609/newsbriefs/wine.html |title=World's Earliest Wine |date=September–October 1996}}</ref> Further evidence shows the [[Mesopotamia]]ns and [[Ancient Egypt]]ians had vine plantations and winemaking skills. [[Greek philosophy|Greek philosophers]] praised the healing powers of grapes both whole and in the form of wine. ''Vitis vinifera'' [[farming|cultivation]] and [[winemaking]] in [[China]] began during the [[Han dynasty]] in the 2nd century<ref>Plocher, T; Rouse, G; Hart, M. (2003). [http://www.northernwinework.com/images/extra/chinatrip/Chinatrip.pdf Discovering Grapes and Wine in the Far North of China] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110714195056/http://www.northernwinework.com/images/extra/chinatrip/Chinatrip.pdf |date=14 July 2011}}</ref> with the importation of the species from [[Ta-Yuan]] ([[Syr Darya river]] valley, [[Uzbekistan]]).  However, wild vine "mountain grapes" like ''[[Vitis thunbergii]]'' were being used for wine making before that time.<ref>Eijkhoff, P. (2000). [http://www.eykhoff.nl/Wine%20in%20China.pdf Wine in China; its history and contemporary developments].</ref> In [[traditional medicine]] of India ''Vitis vinifera'' is used in prescriptions for [[cough]], respiratory tract [[catarrh]], subacute cases of enlarged liver and spleen, as well as in alcohol-based tonics (Aasavs).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=L |last2=Waltenberger |first2=B |last3=Pferschy-Wenzig |first3=EM |last4=Blunder |first4=M |last5=Liu |first5=X |last6=Malainer |first6=C |last7=Blazevic |first7=T |last8=Schwaiger |first8=S |last9=Rollinger |first9=JM |display-authors=8 |year=2014 |title=Natural product agonists of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ): a review |journal=Biochem Pharmacol |volume=92 |issue=1 |pages=73–89 |doi=10.1016/j.bcp.2014.07.018 |pmid=25083916 |pmc=4212005 |bibcode=2014BioPh..92...73W }}</ref>

In the Mediterranean Basin, leaves and young stems are traditionally used to feed sheep and goats after grapevine pruning.<ref>Heuzé V., Thiollet H., Tran G., 2017. Grape leaves and vine shoots. Feedipedia, a programme by INRA, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO. https://www.feedipedia.org/node/512.</ref>

Using the sap of grapevines, European folk healers sought to cure skin and eye diseases. Other historical uses include the [[Leaf|leaves]] being used to stop bleeding, pain and inflammation of [[hemorrhoids]]. Unripe grapes were used for treating sore throats, and raisins were given as treatments for consumption ([[tuberculosis]]), [[constipation]] and [[thirst]]. Ripe grapes were used for the treatment of [[cancer]], [[cholera]], [[smallpox]], [[nausea]], skin and eye infections as well as [[kidney disease|kidney]] and [[liver disease]]s.

Seedless grape varieties were developed to appeal to consumers, but researchers are now discovering that many of the healthful properties of grapes may actually come from the seeds themselves, thanks to their enriched [[phytochemical]] content.<ref>{{cite journal

}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal

Grapevine leaves are filled with minced meat (such as lamb, pork or beef), rice and onions in the making of Balkan traditional [[dolma]].

A popular cultivar in Australia, [[Vitis 'Ornamental Grape'|''Vitis'' 'Ornamental Grape']], derived from ''Vitis vinifera'' × ''[[Vitis rupestris|rupestris]]'', is used in gardens for its impressive foliage that turn brilliant red, [[Scarlet (color)|scarlet]], purple and/or orange in autumn. Originally bred in France, it thrives in a range of climates from hot and dry, to cool moist and subtropical, with different soil types benefitting the plant.<ref>[https://www.yates.com.au/plants/flowers-and-ornamentals/ornamental-grape/how-to-grow-ornamental-grape/ Ornamental Grape] Yates, a division of DuluxGroup (Australia) Pty Ltd.</ref>

=== Climate change ===
{{See also|Effects of climate change on agriculture}}
[[File:Damaged_and_sunburnt_Chardonnay_clusters.JPG|thumb|upright|[[Chardonnay]] grapes which had been damaged by heat from sunburn]]
Grapevines are very responsive to their surrounding environment with a seasonal variation in yield of 32.5%.<ref name="Chloupek2004">{{cite journal | vauthors = Chloupek O, Hrstkova P, Schweigert P | title = Yield and its stability, crop diversity, adaptability and response to climate change, weather and fertilisation over 75 years in the Czech Republic in comparison to some European countries | journal = Field Crops Research | date = February 2004 | volume = 85 | issue = 2–3 | pages = 167–190 | doi = 10.1016/S0378-4290(03)00162-X | bibcode = 2004FCrRe..85..167C }}</ref> Climate is one of the key controlling factors in grape and wine production,<ref name="Fraga2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fraga H, Malheiro AC, Moutinho-Pereira J, Santos JA | title = Climate factors driving wine production in the Portuguese Minho region | journal = Agricultural and Forest Meteorology | date = February 2014 | volume = 15 | issue = 185 | pages = 26–36 | doi = 10.1016/j.agrformet.2013.11.003 | bibcode = 2014AgFM..185...26F }}</ref> affecting the suitability of certain grape varieties to a particular region as well as the type and quality of the wine produced.<ref name="Gladstones1992">{{cite book | vauthors =Gladstones JS |title=Viticulture and Environment: a study of the effects of environment on grapegrowing and wine qualities, with emphasis on present and future areas for growing winegrape in Australia |date=2016 |location=Tanunda, S. Aust. | publisher = Trivinum Press |isbn=978-0-9945016-1-5 |edition=Second | url = http://winebookcellar.com.au/viticulture-environment/ }}</ref><ref name="Fraga2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fraga H, Santos JA, Malheiro AC, Oliveira AA, Moutinho-Pereira J, Jones GV | title = Climatic suitability of Portuguese grapevine varieties and climate change adaptation | journal = International Journal of Climatology | date = January 2016 | volume = 36 | issue = 1 | pages = 1–2 | doi = 10.1002/joc.4325 | bibcode = 2016IJCli..36....1F | s2cid = 140186551 }}</ref> Wine composition is largely dependent on the [[mesoclimate]] and the [[microclimate]] and this means that for high quality wines to be produced, a climate-soil-variety equilibrium has to be maintained. The interaction between climate-soil-variety will in some cases come under threat from the [[effects of climate change]]. Identification of genes underlying [[Phenology|phenological]] variation in grape may help to maintain consistent yield of particular varieties in future climatic conditions.<ref name="Grzeskowiak2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Grzeskowiak L, Costantini L, Lorenzi S, Grando MS | title = Candidate loci for phenology and fruitfulness contributing to the phenotypic variability observed in grapevine | journal = Theoretical and Applied Genetics | volume = 126 | issue = 11 | pages = 2763–76 | date = November 2013 | pmid = 23918063 | pmc = 3825586 | doi = 10.1007/s00122-013-2170-1 }}</ref>

Of all environmental factors, temperature seems to have the most profound effect on viticulture as the temperature during the winter dormancy affects the budding for the following growing season.<ref name="Jones2005">{{cite book | vauthors = Jones GV | date = 2005 | chapter = Climate change in the western United States grape growing regions | title = Proceedings of the Seventh International Symposium on Grapevine Physiology and Biotechnology | pages = 41–59 | veditors = Williams LE }}</ref> Prolonged high temperature can have a negative impact on the quality of the grapes as well as the wine as it affects the development of grape components that give colour, aroma, accumulation of sugar, the loss of acids through respiration as well as the presence of other flavour compounds that give grapes their distinctive traits. Sustained intermediate temperatures and minimal day-to-day variability during the growth and ripening periods are favourable. [[Annual growth cycle of grapevines|Grapevine annual growth cycles]] begin in spring with bud break initiated by consistent day time temperatures of 10 degrees [[Celsius]].<ref name="Winkler1974">{{cite book | vauthors = Winkler A, Cook J, Kliewere W, Lider L | date = 1974 | title = General Viticulture | publisher = University of California Press | location = Berkeley }}</ref> The unpredictable nature of climate change may also bring occurrences of frosts which may occur outside of the usual winter periods. Frosts cause lower yields and effects grape quality due to reduction of bud fruitfulness and therefore grapevine production benefits from frost free periods.

Organic acids are essential in wine quality. The [[phenolic content in wine|phenolic compounds]] such as [[anthocyanin]]s and [[tannin (wine)|tannin]]s help give the wine its colour, bitterness, astringency and anti-oxidant capacity.<ref name="Downey2006">{{cite journal | vauthors = Downey MO, Dokoozlian NK, Krstic MP | title = Cultural practice and environmental impacts on the flavonoid composition of grapes and wine: a review of recent research | journal = American Journal of Enology and Viticulture | date = September 2006 | volume = 57 | issue = 3 | pages = 257–268 | doi = 10.5344/ajev.2006.57.3.257 | s2cid = 97229221 | url = https://www.ajevonline.org/node/5320.full | doi-access = free }}</ref> Research has shown that grapevines exposed to temperature consistently around 30 degrees Celsius had significantly lower concentrations of anthocyanins compared to grapevines exposed to temperatures consistently around 20 degrees Celsius.<ref name="Yamane2006">{{cite journal | vauthors = Yamane T, Jeong ST, Goto-Yamamoto N, Koshita Y, Kobayashi S | title = Effects of temperature on anthocyanin biosynthesis in grape berry skins |journal = American Journal of Enology and Viticulture | date = March 2006 | volume = 57 | issue = 1 | pages = 54–59 | doi = 10.5344/ajev.2006.57.1.54 | s2cid = 83726801 | url = https://www.ajevonline.org/content/57/1/54.short |url-access=subscription}}</ref>  Temperatures around or exceeding 35 degrees Celsius are found to stall anthocyanin production as well as degrade the anthocyanins that are produced.<ref name="Mori2007">{{cite journal | vauthors = Mori K, Goto-Yamamoto N, Kitayama M, Hashizume K | title = Loss of anthocyanins in red-wine grape under high temperature | journal = Journal of Experimental Botany | volume = 58 | issue = 8 | pages = 1935–45 | date = 2007 | pmid = 17452755 | doi = 10.1093/jxb/erm055 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Furthermore, anthocyanins were found to be positively correlated to temperatures between 16–22 degrees Celsius from [[veraison]] (change of colour of the berries) to harvest.<ref name="Nicholas2011">{{cite journal | vauthors = Nicholas KA, Matthews MA, Lobell DB, Willits NH, Field CB | title = Effect of vineyard-scale climate variability on Pinot noir phenolic composition | journal = Agricultural and Forest Meteorology | date = December 2011 | volume = 151 | issue = 12 | pages = 1556–1567 | doi = 10.1016/j.agrformet.2011.06.010 | bibcode = 2011AgFM..151.1556N | s2cid = 86734136 }}</ref> Tannins give wine astringency and a "drying in the mouth" taste and also bind onto anthocyanin to give more stable molecules which are important in giving long term colour in aged [[red wines]].<ref name="Harbertson2003">{{cite journal | vauthors = Harbertson JF, Picciotto EA, Adams DO | title = Measurement of polymeric pigments in grape berry extract sand wines using a protein precipitation assay combined with bisulfite bleaching | journal = American Journal of Enology and Viticulture | date = January 2003 | volume = 54 | issue = 4 | pages = 301–306 | doi = 10.5344/ajev.2003.54.4.301 | s2cid = 87518358 | url = https://www.ajevonline.org/content/54/4/301.short | url-access = subscription }}</ref> As the presence of phenolic compounds in wine are affected heavily by temperature, an increase in average temperatures will affect their presence in wine regions and will therefore affect grape quality.

Altered [[precipitation]] patterns are also anticipated (both annually and seasonally) with rainfall occurrences varying in amount and frequency. Increases in the amount of rainfall have will likely cause an increase in soil erosion; while occasional lack of rainfall, in times when it usually occurs, may result in drought conditions causing stress on grapevines.<ref name="Schultz2000">{{cite journal | vauthors = Schultz HR | title = Climate change and viticulture: a European perspective on climatology, carbon dioxide and UV-B effects | journal = Australian Journal of Grape and Wine Research | date = April 2000 | volume = 6 | issue = 1 | pages = 2–12 | doi = 10.1111/j.1755-0238.2000.tb00156.x }}</ref> Rainfall is critical at the beginning of the growing season for the budburst and [[inflorescence]] development while consistent dry periods are important for the flowering and ripening periods.<ref name="Ramos2008">{{cite journal | vauthors = Ramos MC, Jones GV, Martínez-Casasnovas JA | title = Structure and trends in climate parameters affecting winegrape production in northeast Spain | journal = Climate Research | date = November 2008 | volume = 38 | issue = 1 | pages = 1–5 | doi = 10.3354/cr00759 | bibcode = 2008ClRes..38....1R | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Increased CO<sub>2</sub> levels will likely have an effect on the [[photosynthesis|photosynthetic activity]] in grapevines as photosynthesis is stimulated by a rise in CO<sub>2</sub> and has been known to also lead to an increase leaf area and vegetative dry weight.<ref name="Bindi1996">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bindi M, Fibbi L, Gozzini B, Orlandini S, Seghi L | title = The effect of elevated CO2 concentration on grapevine growth under field conditions | veditors = Poni S, Peterlunger E, Iacono F, Intrieri C | issue = Strategies to Optimize Wine Grape Quality | journal = Acta Horticulturae | volume = 427 | date = July 1995  | pages = 325–330 | doi = 10.17660/ActaHortic.1996.427.38 }}</ref> Raised atmospheric CO<sub>2</sub> is also believed to result in partial [[stoma]]tal closure which indirectly leads to increased leaf temperatures. A rise in leaf temperatures may alter [[RuBisCO|ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase]] (RuBisCo) relationship with carbon dioxide and oxygen which will also affect the plants' photosynthesis capabilities.<ref name="Schultz2000" /> Raised atmospheric carbon dioxide is also known to decrease the stomatal density of some grapevine varieties.<ref name="Moutinho-Pereira2009">{{cite journal | vauthors = Moutinho-Pereira J, Gonçalves B, Bacelar E, Cunha JB, Countinho J, Correira CM | title = Effects of elevated CO2 on grapevine (Vitis vinifera L.): physiological and yield attributes | journal = Vitis-Journal of Grapevine Research | date = April 2015 | volume = 48 | issue = 4 | pages = 159–165 }}</ref>

==== Cultivation variations ====
The gradually increasing temperatures will lead to a shift in suitable growing regions.<ref name="Fraga2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fraga H, García de Cortázar Atauri I, Malheiro AC, Santos JA | title = Modelling climate change impacts on viticultural yield, phenology and stress conditions in Europe | journal = Global Change Biology | volume = 22 | issue = 11 | pages = 3774–3788 | date = November 2016 | pmid = 27254813 | doi = 10.1111/gcb.13382 | bibcode = 2016GCBio..22.3774F | s2cid = 22810514 }}</ref> It is estimated that the northern boundary of European viticulture will shift north {{convert|10|to|30|km|mi}} per decade up to 2020 with a doubling of this rate predicted between 2020 and 2050.<ref name="Kenny1993">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kenny GJ, Harrison PA | title = The effects of climate variability and change on grape suitability in Europe | journal = Journal of Wine Research | date = January 1992 | volume = 3 | issue = 3 | pages = 163–183 | doi =  10.1080/09571269208717931 }}</ref>{{Update inline|date=March 2022}} This has positive and negative effects, as it opens doors to new cultivars being grown in certain regions but a loss of suitability of other cultivars and may also risk production quality and quantity in general.<ref name="Kovacs2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kovacs E, Kopecsko Z, Puskas J | date = 2014 | title = The Impact of Climate Change on Wine Regions of the Western Part of the Carpathian Basin | journal = Proceedings of University of West Hungary Savaria Campus XX. Natural Sciences 15 | location = Szombathely | pages = 71–89 }}</ref><ref name="Fraga2016" />

==== Adapting wine production ====
Systems have been developed to manipulate the temperatures of vines. These include a chamber free system where air can be heated or cooled and then blown across grape bunches to get a {{convert|10|C-change}} differential.<ref name="Tarara2008">{{cite journal | vauthors = Tarara JM, Lee J, Spayd SE, Scagel CF | title = Berry temperature and solar radiation alter acylation, proportion, and concentration of anthocyanin in Merlot grapes | journal = American Journal of Enology and Viticulture | date = September 2008 | volume = 59 | issue = 3 | pages = 235–247 | doi = 10.5344/ajev.2008.59.3.235 | s2cid = 87523932 }}</ref> Mini chambers combined with [[shade cloth]] and reflective foils have also been used to manipulate the temperature and [[irradiance]].<ref name="Petrie2005">{{cite journal | vauthors = Petrie PR, Clingeleffer PR | title = Effects of temperature and light (before and after budburst) on inflorescence morphology and flower number of Chardonnay grapevines (Vitis vinifera L.) | journal = Australian Journal of Grape and Wine Research | date = April 2005 | volume = 11 | issue = 1 | pages = 59–65 | doi = 10.1111/j.1755-0238.2005.tb00279.x | bibcode = 2005AJGWR..11...59P | doi-access = free }}</ref> Using [[polyethylene]] sleeves to cover cordons and canes were also found to increase maximum temperature by {{convert|5-8|C-change}} and decrease minimum temperature by {{convert|1-2|C-change}}.<ref name="Bowen2004">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bowen PA, Bogdanoff CP, Estergaard B | title = Impacts of using polyethylene sleeves and wavelength selective mulch in vineyards. I. Effects on air and soil temperatures and degree day accumulation | journal = Canadian Journal of Plant Science | date = April 2004 | volume = 84 | issue = 2 | pages = 545–553 | doi = 10.4141/P03-093 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

== Genome ==
There is great interest in the genetic diversity of the ''Vitis vinifera'' as it is the world's most important [[perennial]] [[Horticulture|horticultural]] crop, with an estimated value of approximately US$60 billion with more than 6000 cultivated forms. The species has a relatively small genomes of about 500 Mb, similar to  species such as [[Populus|poplar]] (465 Mbp), ''[[Medicago]]'' (500 Mbp), and [[rice]] (430 Mbp). However, [[DNA sequencing|sequencing]] and assembly of their genomes is particularly challenging due to their high [[heterozygosity]], that is, differences between sister [[chromosome]]s (''Vitis'' sp. has 19 chromosome pairs).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cantu |first1=Dario |last2=Massonnet |first2=Mélanie |last3=Cochetel |first3=Noé |date=July 2024 |title=The wild side of grape genomics |journal=Trends in Genetics |language=en |volume=40 |issue=7 |pages=601–612 |doi=10.1016/j.tig.2024.04.014|pmid=38777691 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

There is considerable variation among grape genomes. For instance, the genome of the ''Vitis vinifera'' cultivar Mgaloblishvili is much larger than that of V. vinifera ssp. ''vinifera,'' with a genome size of 986 Mbp, encoding 58,912 predicted protein-coding genes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ricciardi |first1=Valentina |last2=Minio |first2=Andrea |last3=Massonnet |first3=Melanie |last4=Wittenberg |first4=Alexander H J |last5=Figueroa-Balderas |first5=Rosa |last6=Maghradze |first6=David |last7=Toffolatti |first7=Silvia Laura |last8=Failla |first8=Osvaldo |last9=Cantu |first9=Dario |last10=De Lorenzis |first10=Gabriella |date=2025-02-20 |title=The genome of Vitis vinifera cv. Mgaloblishvili reveals resistance and susceptibility factors to downy mildew in the Rpv29 and Rpv31 loci |url=https://academic.oup.com/hr/advance-article/doi/10.1093/hr/uhaf055/8026355 |journal=Horticulture Research |volume=12 |issue=6 |article-number=uhaf055 |doi=10.1093/hr/uhaf055 |pmid=40271452 |issn=2662-6810|doi-access=free |pmc=12017795 }}</ref> For comparison, the [[human genome]] only encodes about 20,000 protein-coding genes.

=== Phenolics ===

=== Other chemicals ===
Monoterpenes are present in grape, above all acyclic [[linalool]], [[geraniol]], [[nerol]], [[citronellol]], [[homotrienol]] and monocyclic α-[[terpineol]], mostly occurring as glycosides. Carotenoids accumulate in ripening grape berries. Oxidation of carotenoids produces volatile fragments, C13-[[norisoprenoid]]s. These are strongly odoriferous compounds, such as β-[[ionone]] (aroma of viola), [[damascenone]] (aroma of exotic fruits), β-[[damascone]] (aroma of rose) and β-[[ionol]] (aroma of flowers and fruits).  [[Melatonin]], an alkaloid, has been identified in grape.<ref>{{cite journal |pmid=19445314 |volume=4 |issue=5 |title=Bioactivity of grape chemicals for human health |journal=Natural Product Communications |date=May 2009 |pages=611–34 |last1=Iriti |first1=M |last2=Faoro |first2=F |doi=10.1177/1934578X0900400502 |s2cid=39638336 |doi-access=free}}</ref> In addition, seeds are rich in [[Unsaturated fat|unsaturated fatty acids]], which helps lower levels of total [[cholesterol]] and [[LDL]] cholesterol in the blood.<ref name=":0" />
